title: Formal writing
cando: write formal letters, emails and short reports in the right register

about.text: In this lesson you make a formal phone call, and then you put what you want in writing. You learn how to make your English more formal without making it hard to read, and you read a formal letter and a short report. At the end, you write a report that recommends one of two options, and you present it.
goals: Make a formal call: I'm calling regarding… I'll put that in writing.
Turn up the formality: full forms, formal words and the passive.
Link formal ideas with in which case, at which point and whereby.
Write a formal letter with the right layout, greeting and ending.
Write and present a short report that recommends one of two options.

chapters.title: A call before a letter
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you write formally: letters, emails and short reports.
But first, a phone call. Amina manages the office of a small design studio. The company van needs a parking permit, and the council has refused it. She calls to find out why.
Listen to how she starts. I'm calling on behalf of Brightside Design, regarding our application. Regarding is a formal way to say about.
The officer can't change the decision on the phone. So Amina says: I'll put it in writing. A letter gives both sides a record of what was asked, and when.
Notice the useful phone phrases too. Could you put me through? Please hold the line. Could you give me a reference for this call?

chapters.title: Turning up the formality
chapters.text:
Now the grammar. Formality isn't one switch. It works more like a set of dials.
Dial one: full forms. Not we haven't, but we have not.
Dial two: formal words. Not ask, but enquire. Not tell, but notify.
Dial three: the passive. Not we've received your form, but your form has been received. Notices use the passive all the time. Visitors are asked to sign in. This door must be kept closed.
But don't turn every dial up. Very long sentences and old-fashioned words make a letter hard to read.
Then, formal links. In which case means if that happens. You may appeal, in which case the decision will be reviewed. Whereby means by which. The council has a scheme whereby businesses can pay monthly.

chapters.title: A letter and a report
chapters.text:
Next, you read two documents: the council's reply to Amina, and a short report that she wrote for her director.
Look at the layout. The letter has a heading, so you know at once what it's about. The report has numbered sections, and bullet points for each option.
Then you write your own formal letter. Remember the pairs. Dear Sir or Madam goes with Yours faithfully. Dear Ms Yusuf goes with Yours sincerely.
Finally, test your letter on a reader. Can they say, in one sentence, what you want? If they can't, rewrite it.

chapters.title: Recommending one option
chapters.text:
Then you write and present a short report. You compare two options, and you recommend one. It could be two suppliers, two venues for a staff event, or two phone contracts.
Keep the shape simple: the purpose, option A, option B, and your recommendation.
For each option, give the cost, one advantage and one disadvantage. Then choose. A report that recommends nothing doesn't help anybody.
When you present it, speak more simply than you write. Say we and you. Finish with one clear next step, and a date.
Then take questions. If you don't know an answer, say so, and offer to find out.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer story or article linked to formal writing.
Read it once for the main events. Then read it again, and notice who writes to whom, and whether the writing works for its reader.
Look at the choices each writer makes: the greeting, the layout and the words.

warmup.prompt: You want to complain about a wrong bill. What do you do first?
choices: send an email or a letter
post about it on social media
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people phone first to find out the facts, and then put the complaint in writing, so that there is a record.

conversation.title: A call to the council
conversation.setting: Amina Yusuf is the office manager at Brightside Design, a small design studio. The council has refused their application for a parking permit for the company van, and Amina calls to find out why.
lines: Good morning, Kingsmere Council. How can I help?
Good morning. I've been trying to get through to Parking Services all morning. Could you put me through, please?
Hello. My name's Amina Yusuf. I'm calling on behalf of Brightside Design, regarding our application for a business parking permit.
Of course. Could I take your account number?
Thank you. I'm afraid the application was refused on the third of March. The documentation didn't show that the van is used for work.
We were never notified of that. May I enquire what the status of the application is now?
The file has been closed. But you can appeal in writing within 28 days, in which case the decision will be reviewed by a senior officer.
Is there no way to resolve this over the phone? The van is used for deliveries every day.
I'm afraid I don't have the authority to change the decision. But I can assure you that your appeal will be looked at carefully, and your records will be kept confidential.
In that case, I'll put it in writing today, with our insurance and delivery records. Could you give me a reference for this call?
Certainly. It's P, two two nine one. Thank you for your cooperation, Ms Yusuf.

questions.a: The documents didn't show that the van is used for work.
questions.why: Daniel says the documentation didn't show that the van is used for work.

questions.q: What happens if Amina appeals in writing within 28 days?
questions.a: A senior officer reviews the decision.
wrong: The permit is issued at once.
questions.why: Daniel says: in which case the decision will be reviewed by a senior officer.

questions.q: Why can't Daniel change the decision on the phone?
wrong: The time to appeal has ended.
Amina doesn't know her account number.
questions.why: Daniel says: I don't have the authority to change the decision.

phrases.use: Saying who you are calling for.
Saying, formally, what the call is about.

phrases.text: Could you put me through to…?
phrases.use: Asking to be connected to the right person or department.

phrases.text: May I enquire what the status is?
I don't have the authority to…
phrases.use: Saying that a decision is not yours to make.
Promising something, so the other person doesn't worry.
Saying you will send a letter or an email, so there is a record.

phrases.text: Could you give me a reference for this call?
phrases.use: Getting a record of the call, to quote later.

items.meaning: For another person or an organisation, as their representative.
items.example: I'm writing on behalf of my father, who is in hospital.

items.meaning: To ask for information. It is more formal than ask.
items.example: I am writing to enquire about the position on your website.

items.meaning: To tell somebody something officially.
items.example: You will be notified of the decision by email.

items.meaning: To manage to speak to somebody on the phone.
items.example: I finally got through to the bank after forty minutes.

items.meaning: To wait on the phone until somebody can speak to you.
items.example: Please hold the line while I transfer your call.

items.meaning: A person who speaks or acts for a company or a group.
items.example: A representative from the insurance company will visit on Monday.

items.meaning: The power to make a decision. The local authority is the council for your area.
items.example: Only the manager has the authority to approve a refund.

items.meaning: The number that a bank, a company or a council uses for your account.
items.example: Please quote your account number in every letter.

items.meaning: Official papers that prove or explain something.
items.example: You'll need documentation that shows your address, such as a recent bill.

items.meaning: The situation of something at a particular time, such as an order or an application.
items.example: You can check the status of your order online.

items.meaning: A formal request to change an official decision.
items.example: Her appeal against the parking fine was successful.

items.meaning: To find an answer to a problem, or to end a disagreement.
items.example: We hope to resolve the matter within ten working days.

items.meaning: To tell somebody firmly that something is true, so that they don't worry.
items.example: I can assure you that your payment has been received.

items.meaning: Being willing to help and to work with others.
items.example: Thank you for your cooperation during the building work.

items.meaning: Private, and not to be shared with other people.
items.example: Everything you tell us will be kept confidential.

sound.title: The weak words in a passive
sound.explain: In a passive, the small words before the main verb are weak and quick. Has been sounds like 'z-bin', and will be sounds like 'l-bee'. The stress goes on the main verb. Say the small words quietly, but never leave them out: they carry the tense. Listen, then say each group and line.
groups: has been received · has been refused · has been closed
will be reviewed · will be notified · will be kept
lines: The decision will be reviewed by a senior officer.
Your records will be kept confidential.

sayIt.instructions: Say Amina's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Do you sound calm, polite and clear, like someone who expects a proper answer?
lines: Good morning. I've been trying to get through to Parking Services all morning. Could you put me through, please?
I'm calling on behalf of Brightside Design, regarding our application for a business parking permit.
We were never notified of that. May I enquire what the status of the application is now?
In that case, I'll put it in writing today, with our insurance and delivery records.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the call. They are more formal than everyday English. Three of them use the passive.
examples: I'm calling on behalf of Brightside Design, regarding our application for a business parking permit.
I'm afraid the application was refused on the third of March.
You can appeal in writing within 28 days, in which case the decision will be reviewed by a senior officer.
Your records will be kept confidential.
spot.question: Which words make these sentences formal? Find the three passives. And what does in which case mean?
spot.answer: On behalf of and regarding are formal ways to say for and about. The passives are was refused, will be reviewed and will be kept: they put the application, the decision and the records first, because the thing matters more than the person. In which case means 'if that happens': if you appeal, the decision will be reviewed.

rules.title: The dials of formality, and the passive in notices
rule: Formality has dials. Turn up the ones you need, not all of them.
Full forms and formal words: we haven't → we have not; ask → enquire; tell → notify.
The passive puts the thing first: We've received your form → Your form has been received.
Notices use the passive: Visitors are asked to sign in. This door must be kept closed.
Keep sentences short, and keep 'you'. Formal is not the same as difficult.
rules.mistake: Too far: The undersigned is in receipt of your correspondence. Better: Thank you for your letter.

rules.title: Formal links: in which case, at which point, whereby
rule: In which case = if that happens, then: You may appeal, in which case the decision will be reviewed.
At which point = and at that moment: No reply was received by 14 May, at which point the file was closed.
Whereby = by which, through which: The council has a scheme whereby businesses pay monthly.
Put a comma before in which case and at which point. Whereby follows a noun: a scheme, a system, an agreement.
They belong in letters and reports. In a friendly email, they sound stiff.
rules.mistake: Too stiff for a colleague: Your file arrived, at which point I read it. Better: Your file arrived, and I've read it.

practice.q: Formal letter: I am writing to ___ about the vacancy.
practice.why: Enquire is the formal verb for ask.

practice.q: Notice: Visitors ___ to sign in at reception.
practice.why: Notices use the passive: the visitors are the ones who are asked.

practice.q: Your application ___ received and passed to our assessment team.
practice.why: Present perfect passive: has been + past participle.

practice.q: You may appeal, ___ the decision will be reviewed by a senior officer.
practice.why: In which case means 'if that happens, then'.

practice.q: No reply had been received by 14 May, ___ the file was closed.
practice.why: At which point means 'and at that moment'.

practice.q: The company runs a scheme ___ staff can buy a bicycle and pay for it monthly.
practice.why: Whereby follows a noun (a scheme) and means 'by which'.

practice.q: Notice: This door must ___ closed at all times.
Which sentence is right for a formal letter?
options: I would be grateful for a reply by Friday.
Can you get back to me by Friday?
Drop me a line by Friday, yeah?
practice.a: I would be grateful for a reply by Friday.
practice.why: It uses full forms and a polite formal phrase.

practice.q: Make it formal. We'll tell you our decision soon. → You ___ of our decision within 14 days.
practice.why: The passive puts the reader first: you will be notified.

practice.q: The permit ___ refused because the documents were incomplete.
practice.why: Past simple passive: was + past participle, for a finished event.

yourTurn.prompt: Your office, your gym or your block of flats needs a notice. Write three or four formal lines. Use one passive with must be, one with are asked to, and one sentence with in which case.
yourTurn.model: Residents are asked to keep the main door closed at all times. Bicycles must be stored in the bike room, not in the hallway. Rubbish must be taken to the bins by 8 a.m. on Tuesdays. Items left in the hallway may be removed, in which case they can be collected from the caretaker's office.

text.title: A letter from the council, and a short report
text.body:
PRACTICE DOCUMENTS: this council and this company do not exist

Kingsmere Council · Parking Services
Town Hall, Market Street, Kingsmere KM1 4AA

12 March

Ms A. Yusuf
Office Manager, Brightside Design
14 Canal Street, Kingsmere KM2 9BD

Dear Ms Yusuf

Your appeal: business parking permit (reference P2291)

Thank you for your letter of 5 March. Your appeal has been reviewed by a senior officer, together with the documents you enclosed.

I am pleased to tell you that your appeal has been successful. A business parking permit has been issued for your van, and it is enclosed with this letter. It is valid for twelve months.

Please note that each permit covers one vehicle only. You may apply for a second permit, in which case the same documentation will be required.

The council also runs a scheme whereby small businesses can pay for permits in monthly instalments. Details can be found on our website.

Thank you for your patience while your appeal was considered.

Yours sincerely

Daniel Okafor
Parking Services Officer

---

REPORT: PARKING FOR A SECOND VAN
To: Carlos Mendes, Director
From: Amina Yusuf, Office Manager
Date: 20 March

1. Purpose
This report evaluates two options for parking our second van, which arrives in May, and makes a recommendation.

2. Option A: a second council permit
• Cost: £480 a year, which can be paid monthly.
• The van would be parked outside the studio, where it is loaded.
• A new application must be made, and a decision can take up to four weeks.

3. Option B: a space in Riverside Car Park
• Cost: £75 a month (£900 a year).
• The space is covered and secure, but it is a ten-minute walk from the studio.
• A minimum contract of six months is required.

4. Recommendation
Option A is recommended. It costs just over half as much as Option B, and it is far more practical for loading. If Option A is chosen, the application should be made by 1 April, so that the permit is in place before the van arrives.

gist.a: the council's decision on Brightside's appeal
wrong: a new parking fine for Brightside
gist.why: The letter says the appeal has been successful.

gist.a: It compares two options and recommends one.
wrong: It complains about the council's decision.
It asks the director to buy a second van.
gist.why: Section 1 says it evaluates two options and makes a recommendation.

detail.q: What did the council send with its letter?
detail.why: The letter says the permit has been issued and is enclosed.

detail.q: What must Brightside do to get a permit for a second van?
detail.a: apply again, with the same documents
wrong: ask for the first permit to cover both vans
phone the council and quote the reference
detail.why: Each permit covers one vehicle, and a second application needs the same documentation.

detail.q: What is one disadvantage of Option B?
detail.a: It is a ten-minute walk from the studio.
wrong: The space is not covered or secure.
A decision can take up to four weeks.
detail.why: The report says the space is secure, but a ten-minute walk away.

detail.q: If Option A is chosen, by when should the application be made?
wrong: when the van arrives in May
detail.why: The recommendation says: by 1 April, so the permit is in place before the van arrives.

items.meaning: The greeting at the start of a formal letter when you don't know the reader's name. Write it with capitals: Dear Sir or Madam.
items.example: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to enquire about your evening courses.

items.meaning: The formal ending for a letter that starts Dear Sir or Madam.
items.example: If you begin with Dear Sir or Madam, end with Yours faithfully.

items.meaning: The formal ending for a letter that starts with the reader's name, such as Dear Ms Yusuf.
items.example: She began the letter Dear Mr Patel, so she ended it Yours sincerely.

items.meaning: Sent in the same envelope as a letter, or attached to the same email.
items.example: Please find enclosed a copy of my certificate.

items.meaning: The title at the top of a letter, a page or a section.
items.example: Give the letter a short heading, so the reader knows at once what it's about.

items.meaning: A small dot at the start of each item in a list.
items.example: List the costs of each option as bullet points.

items.meaning: The way text is arranged on a page.
items.example: A clear layout makes a long report much easier to read.

items.meaning: A short form of a word or a phrase, such as asap for 'as soon as possible'.
items.example: Avoid abbreviations like pls and thx in a formal email.

items.meaning: Very informal words, used mainly in speech between friends.
items.example: Don't use slang like quid or a fiver in a letter of complaint.

items.meaning: Advice about what somebody should do, especially at the end of a report.
items.example: The report ends with a clear recommendation.

items.meaning: To study something carefully and decide how good or useful it is.
items.example: We evaluated both suppliers before we made a decision.

model.title: A formal letter of appeal
model.body:
Brightside Design
14 Canal Street
Kingsmere KM2 9BD

5 March

Parking Services
Kingsmere Council
Town Hall, Market Street
Kingsmere KM1 4AA

Dear Sir or Madam

Appeal: business parking permit, account number 40 71 26 38

I am writing on behalf of Brightside Design to appeal against the decision to refuse our application for a business parking permit. I spoke to Parking Services about this on 5 March (call reference P2291).

I understand that the application was refused because our documentation did not show that the van is used for work. The van is used every day to deliver finished work to our clients, and there is nowhere else to park it near our studio.

Please find enclosed:
• a copy of the van's business insurance
• our delivery records for January and February

The decision is dated 3 February, but we were never notified of it, and only learned of it when we called. I would therefore be grateful if the 28 days for this appeal could be counted from 5 March.

Thank you for considering this appeal. If any further information is needed, I can be contacted on 01632 960 418.

Yours faithfully

Amina Yusuf
Office Manager, Brightside Design

write.task: Write a formal letter of 150 to 200 words. Choose one: an appeal against a decision (a fine or a refused application), a formal complaint, or a request for information. Use a heading and the right greeting and ending. Then test it on a reader: give it to a colleague, your teacher or Wehel, and ask them to say in one sentence what you want. If they can't, rewrite it.
write.starter: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to …
checklist: I used a heading and the right pair: Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully, or Dear Ms … Yours sincerely.
I used no contractions, no slang and no abbreviations.
I said clearly what I want, and what I have enclosed.
My reader could say in one sentence what my letter asks for.

card.title: Recommend one option
card.situation: Your manager, your residents' group or your family has to choose between two options: two suppliers, two venues for a staff event, two phone contracts, or repairing an old machine or buying a new one. You have been asked to evaluate both and recommend one.
card.goal: Write a short report with four headings: Purpose, Option A, Option B and Recommendation. Then present it in two minutes, and answer questions.

phrases: The purpose of this report is to compare … and …
Option A has two main advantages. First, … Second, …
Having evaluated both options, I recommend …
If Option A is chosen, the next step is to … by …
I'm happy to take any questions.
prepare.notes: Make a table first: the cost, the advantages and the disadvantages of each option. Then choose ONE recommendation, with one next step and a date. When you present, speak more simply than you write: use we and you, and keep your sentences short.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, present your report in two minutes. The class are the managers who must decide: they ask you questions, and then they vote for an option.
doIt.wehel: You are my manager. I will give you a short report that compares two options and recommends one. Read it, then ask me three questions about it, one at a time. After that, tell me if my report is formal enough, and correct two of my sentences. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Presenting the report
lines: Thanks for your time, Carlos. I'd like to present my report on parking for the second van. There are two options.
Option A is a second council permit. It costs four hundred and eighty pounds a year, and it can be paid monthly.
And the van would be parked outside the studio?
Exactly, and that's the main advantage: it's parked where it's loaded. Option B is a space in Riverside Car Park, at seventy-five pounds a month.
That's nine hundred a year. What do we get for the extra money?
A covered, secure space. However, it's a ten-minute walk away, and there's a minimum contract of six months.
Having evaluated both options, I recommend Option A. It costs just over half as much, and it's far more practical.
What if the council refuses the application?
Good question. In that case, there would still be time to take Option B, as long as we apply by the first of April.
Fine. Put the recommendation in writing, and I'll sign it off.
I'll send you the final version this afternoon.
compare: Did you say the purpose of the report first?
Did you give the cost, one advantage and one disadvantage of each option?
Did you make one clear recommendation, with a next step and a date?
Was your written report formal, and your talk clear and simple?

canDo: I can make a formal phone call and say that I'll put it in writing.
I can make a text more formal: full forms, formal words and the passive.
I can link formal ideas with in which case, at which point and whereby.
I can write a formal letter with the right layout, greeting and ending.
I can write and present a short report that recommends one option.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who is writing, and to whom? Why do you think they chose to write rather than call?
reading.talk: Was the writing in the story too formal, too informal, or right for its reader? Think of a letter or an email you once found hard to understand. What would you change? Write a short paragraph, or talk about it with Wehel.

quiz.q: A letter that starts Dear Sir or Madam ends with ___ .
quiz.why: No name at the start means Yours faithfully at the end.

quiz.q: Please find ___ a copy of my passport.
quiz.why: Please find enclosed is the formal way to say what you have sent.

quiz.q: Notice: Mobile phones must ___ switched off during the exam.
You may ask for a review, ___ your file will be sent to a senior officer.
quiz.why: In which case means 'if that happens, then'.

quiz.q: The bank has a system ___ customers can freeze their card in the app.
quiz.why: Whereby follows a noun (a system) and means 'by which'.

quiz.q: I'm calling ___ my father, who can't come to the phone.
quiz.why: On behalf of means for somebody, as their representative.

quiz.q: Which sentence is right for a formal report?
options: The costs have been checked twice.
We've double-checked the costs, no worries.
quiz.a: The costs have been checked twice.
quiz.why: It uses a full form, the passive, and no slang or abbreviations.

quiz.q: We'll give you a discount ___ you order at least 200 units.
quiz.why: Provided that means 'only if': the discount depends on the order.

quiz.q: The plan is expensive. ___, it will save money in the long run.
quiz.why: Even so answers a weak point: it is true, but this matters more.

quiz.q: The deadline has moved to Monday. ___ we have two extra days.
quiz.why: This means that points back to the last sentence and gives its result.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the phone call in pairs, then change the reason for calling: a wrong bill, a refund, a refused application. Then say an everyday message together, and turn up the formality one dial at a time.
Day 2: the report task. Each learner presents a two-option report in two minutes. The class asks questions and votes, and you give feedback on the register.
Day 3: talk about the book. Then learners swap their formal letters and test them: can the reader say in one sentence what the letter asks for?
